¶
'''bedlar†''', '''bedlawer†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedlawere'' (= G. ''bettlager''), < ''bed'' + *''lawer'', appar. < Icel. ''lag'', a lying; cf. ''lair.''] A bedridden person. [Old English and Scotch.]

'''bedless''' (bed′les), ''a.'' [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] Without a bed.

'''bed-linen''' (bed′lin″en), ''n.'' Sheets, pillow-cases, etc., originally always of linen, now sometimes of cotton.

'''bed-lounge''' (bed′lounj), ''n.'' A combined bed and lounge; a lounge or plain sofa made so as to open and form a bed.

'''bedmaker''' (bed′mā″kėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedmaker.''] '''1.''' One who manufactures beds or bedsteads. —'''2.''' One who prepares beds for use; especially, in English universities, a man or woman whose duty it is to take care of the rooms and make the beds in college. Female bedmakers were forbidden in Cambridge in 1625, but are now usual.
{{smaller block|The ''bed-makers'' are the women who take care of the rooms; there is about one to each staircase, that is to say, to every eight rooms.{{right|''C. A. Bristed'', English University, p. 30.}}}}

'''bedmate''' (bed′māt), ''n.'' A bedfellow. ''Shak.''

'''bed-molding''' (bed′mōl″ding), ''n.'' In ''arch.'', a molding of the cornice of an entablature, situ-

{{smaller block|even exciting, exceptions to the common routine.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 246.}}}}

'''2.''' A vagabond boy; a street Arab.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Relating to the Bedouins.

'''bed-pan''' (bed′pan), ''n.'' '''1.''' A pan for warming beds; a warming-pan.—'''2.''' A necessary utensil for the use of persons confined to bed.

'''bedpheer†, bedphere†,''' ''n.'' Erroneous spellings of ''bedfere.''

'''bed-plate, bed-piece''' (bed′plāt, -pēs), ''n.'' In ''mech.'', the sole-plate or foundation-plate of an engine, etc.

'''bedpost''' (bed′pōst), ''n.'' '''1†.''' Same as ''bedstaff.''—'''2.''' A post forming an angle of a bedstead, in old bedsteads often rising high enough to support the canopy and rods for the curtain.—{{smaller|'''In the twinkling of a bedpost,''' with the utmost rapidity. See ''bedstaff.''}}

'''bed-presser''' (bed′pres″ėr), ''n.'' A lazy fellow; one who loves his bed.
{{smaller block|This sanguine coward, this ''bed-presser'', this horse-back breaker, this huge hill of flesh. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.}}}}

'''bedquilt''' (bed′kwilt), ''n.'' A wadded and quilted covering for a bed. Also used for ''bedspread''
readings.c2s4:
and ''comforter.''
{{smaller block|The king [in a Sicilian fairy-story] issues a proclamation promising a large reward to whoever shall steal the ''bed-quilt'' of a certain ogre.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 34.}}}}

'''bedrabble''' (bē-drab′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drabble.''] To make wet and dirty with rain and mud. ''Kingsley.''

'''bedraggle''' (bẹ̄-drag′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''draggle.''] To soil or wet by dragging in dirt, mud, moist places, etc., as the bottom of a garment in walking; cause to appear wet and limp, as a flag when rained upon.

'''bedral<sup>1</sup>''' (bed′ral), ''n.'' [Also ''bethral, betherel''; appar. a corruption of ''beadle'', var. ''beddel'', Sc. ''beddal'', etc.] A beadle. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|I’ll hae her before presbytery and synod; I’m half a minister mysel’, now that I’m ''bedral'' in an inhabited parish.
{{right|''Scott'', Bride of Lammermoor, xxxiv.}}}}

'''bedral<sup>2</sup>†''' (bed′ral), ''n.'' [Also ''bedrel'', a corruption of ''bedred'', for ''bedrid'': see ''bedrid.''] A per-
readings.c3s1:
son who is bedridden. ''Knox.'' Also ''bed-thrall.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>His father—who as ''Bedrel'' lay
Before his gate. {{right|''Douglas'', tr. of Virgil.}}</poem>}}

'''bedreint†.''' Obsolete past participle of ''bedrench.''

'''bedrench''' (bẹ̄-drench′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''bedrenchen'' (pp. ''bedreint''); < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drench.''] To drench thoroughly; soak; saturate with moisture.
{{smaller block|Receyve our billes with teres al ''bedreynt.''
{{right|''Court of Love'', l. 577.}}
<poem>Such crimson tempest should ''bedrench''
The fresh green lap of fair King Richard’s land.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 3.}}}}

'''bedress''' (bẹ̄-dres′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dress.''] To dress up.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Bride whose tonish inclination
Attended to the ruling fashion,
To make her entry had ''bedress’d''
Her upright form in all her best.</poem>
{{right|''W. Combe'', Dr. Syntax in Search of a Wife, v.}}}}

'''bedridden, bedrid''' (bed′rid″n, -rid), ''a.'' [< ME. ''bedred, bedrede, bedreden, bedredden,'' adj. and n., < AS. ''bedreda, bedrida, bedryda, beddredda,'' n., one bedridden, lit. a bed-rider (< ''bed,'' bed, + ''rida, ridda,'' a rider, a knight, < ''rīdan,'' ride). Cf. LG. ''bedderede, bedderedig,'' bedridden; OHG. ''pettiriso,'' G. ''bettrise,'' of same sense. The second element came to be regarded as the pp. of ''ride;'' hence the now usual form ''bedridden,'' ME. ''bedreden.''] Confined to bed by age, infirmity, or sickness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Is not your father grown incapable
Of reasonable affairs? . . .
Lies he not ''bed-rid?'' {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3.}}</poem>
What an over-worne and ''bedrid'' Argument is this!
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

2. A room or apartment containing or intended to contain a bed; a sleeping-apartment.

'''bedrop''' (bē-drop′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedropped'' (sometimes ''bedropt''), ppr. ''bedropping''. [< ME. ''bedroppen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drop''.] '''1.''' To drop upon; fall upon in drops.
{{smaller block|<poem>As men sene the dew ''bedroppe''
The leves and the flowers eke.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., iii. 254.}}}}
'''2.''' To cover, strew, or sprinkle with drops, or as if with drops; bespatter; bespangle.
{{smaller block|<poem>The yellow carp, in scales ''bedropp’d'' with gold.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 144.}}
<poem>Rueful cheek,
Pale and ''bedropped'' with ever-flowing tears.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, ix.}}}}

'''bed-sacking''' (bed′sak″ing), ''n.'' Canvas designed to be stretched on the framework of a bedstead to support the mattresses and bedclothes.

'''bed-screw''' (bed′skrö), ''n.'' '''1.''' A bed-key or bed-wrench.—'''2.''' Same as ''barrel-screw''.

'''bedside''' (bed′sīd), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedsyde'', orig. ''beddes side'', i. e., bed’s side.] The side of a bed; position by a bed: usually with reference to attendance on one confined to bed: as, she watched by his ''bedside'' till dawn.

'''bedsister†''' (bed′sis″tėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bedsuster'' (Robert of Gloucester), < ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''suster'', sister.] A concubine.
{{smaller block|It is not much to be wondered at that we lost ''bed-sister'' for concubine. {{right|''F. Hall'', Mod. Eng., p. 165, note.}}}}

'''bed-sore''' (bed′sōr), ''n.'' A very troublesome kind of ulcer, liable to appear on patients long confined in bed and either unable or not allowed

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bedight|500|bed-sore}}</noinclude><poem>Many a rare and sumptuous tome
In vellum bound, with gold ''bedight''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Longfellow'', Wayside Inn, Prelude.}}}}

'''bedim''' (bē-dim′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedimmed'', ppr. ''bedimming''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dim''.]   To make dim; obscure or darken; becloud.

{{smaller block|I have ''bedimm’d'' the noontide sun. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Phœbe, coming so suddenly from the sunny daylight, was altogether ''bedimmed'' in such density of shadow as lurked in most of the passages of the old house.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xx.}}}}

'''bedimple''' (bē-dim′pl), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dimple''.]   To cover over or mark with dimples.

'''bedirt†''' (bē-dėrt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dirt''.]   To defile with dirt; figuratively, throw dirt at; vilify.

'''bedismal''' (bē-diz′mal), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedismaled'' or ''bedismalled'', ppr. ''bedismaling'' or ''bedismalling''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dismal''.]   To make dismal.

'''bedizen''' (bē-diz′n or -dī′zn), ''v. t.''   [Also sometimes ''bedizzen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dizen''.]   To deck or dress out, especially in a tawdry manner or with vulgar finery.

{{smaller block|Remnants of tapestried hangings, window curtains, and shreds of pictures, with which he had ''bedizened'' his tatters.
{{right|''Scott'', Waverley, II. xxvii.}}}}

{{smaller block|A colossal image of the Virgin, . . . ''bedizened'' and effulgent, was borne aloft upon the shoulders of her adorers.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 556.}}}}

<poem>Like clouds which ''bedizen''
At sunset the western horizon.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', The Glove.}}}}

'''bedizenment''' (bē-diz′n- or -dī′zn-ment), ''n.''   [< ''bedizen'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of bedizening; the state of being bedizened; that which bedizens.

{{smaller block|The ''bedizenment'' of the great spirit’s sanctuary with . . . skulls. {{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho! p. 451.}}}}
{{smaller block|Strong Dames of the Market, . . . with oak-branches, tricolor ''bedizenment''. {{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., III. iv. 4.}}}}

'''bed-key''' (bed′kē), ''n.'' Same as ''bed-wrench.''

'''bedlam''' (bed′lam), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bedlem'', ''bethlem'', < ME. ''bedlem'', ''bedleem'', ''bethlem'', a corruption of ''Bethlehem'' (ME. ''Bethleem'', ''Bedlem''): see ''Bethlehem''. See def. 1.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' [''cap.''] The hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem in London, originally a priory, founded about 1247, but afterward used as an asylum for lunatics.
{{smaller block|At my returne I stept into ''Bedlame'', where I saw several poore miserable creatures in chaines. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, April 21, 1657.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' A madhouse; a lunatic asylum.
{{smaller block|<poem>He’s past
Recovery; a ''Bedlam'' cannot cure him.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, v. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' A scene of wild uproar and confusion.
{{smaller block|A general division of possessions would make the country a scene of profligate extravagance for one year and of universal desolation the next—a ''bedlam'' for one short season and a charnel-house ever after. {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
'''4†.''' An inmate or a patient of Bethlehem Hospital, or Bedlam; specifically, one discharged as cured (though often only partially cured) and licensed to beg. {{smaller|Such persons wore a tin plate as a badge on their left arm, and were known as ''bedlam beggars'', ''bedlamites'', or ''bedlamers''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let’s follow the old earl, and get the ''Bedlam''
To lead him where he would; his roguish madness
Allows itself to anything.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 7.}}}}
Hence—'''5†.''' In general, a madman; a lunatic. {{smaller|—'''Jack''' or '''Tom o’ Bedlam''', a madman.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Belonging to or fit for a bedlam or madhouse; mad; mentally deranged.
{{smaller block|The ''bedlam'' brain-sick duchess. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|This which followes is plaine ''bedlam'' stuffe, this is the Demoniack legion indeed.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Bedlam beggar.''' See I., 4.}}

'''bedlamer''' (bed′lam-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bedlam'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A bedlam beggar. See ''bedlam'', ''n.'', 4.
{{smaller block|This country [the Border] was then much troubled with ''Bedlamers.'' {{right|''Roger North'', Lord Guilford, I. 271.}}}}
'''2.''' The name given by seal-hunters to the hooded seal, ''Cystophora cristata'', when a year old, from its frantic cries and actions when it cannot escape its pursuers.

'''bedlamism''' (bed′lam-izm), ''n.''   [< ''bedlam'' + ''-ism.'']   A word or act which is characteristic of madness or of mad people; a trait of madness.   ''Carlyle.''

'''bedlamite''' (bed′lam-īt), ''n.''   [< ''bedlam'' + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   A madman. See ''bedlam'', ''n.'', 4.
{{smaller block|What means the ''Bedlamite'' by this freak?
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Twice-Told Tales, II.}}}}

'''bedlamitish''' (bed′lam-īt-ish), ''a.''   [< ''bedlamite'' + ''-ish.'']   Resembling or characteristic of a bedlamite or madman.
{{smaller block|Their ''Bedlamitish'' creation of needless noises.
{{right|''Carlyle'', in Froude, II. 236.}}}}

'''bedlamize''' (bed′lam-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedlamized'', ppr. ''bedlamizing''. To make mad. {{smaller block|The Germans, on their part, calmly conscious of their irresistible strength, proceeded to fasten ever more compulsive bonds and sobering straps on the ''Bedlamised'' country.{{right|''Lowe'', Bismarck, I. 599.}}}}

'''bedlar†''', '''bedlawer†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''bedlawere'' (= G. ''bettlager''), < ''bed'' + *''lawer'', appar. < Icel. ''lag'', a lying; cf. ''lair.'']   A bedridden person. [Old English and Scotch.]

'''bedless''' (bed′les), ''a.''   [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   Without a bed.

'''bed-linen''' (bed′lin″en), ''n.'' Sheets, pillow-cases, etc., originally always of linen, now sometimes of cotton.

'''bed-lounge''' (bed′lounj), ''n.'' A combined bed and lounge; a lounge or plain sofa made so as to open and form a bed.

'''bedmaker''' (bed′mā″kėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bedmaker.'']   '''1.''' One who manufactures beds or bedsteads. —'''2.''' One who prepares beds for use; especially, in English universities, a man or woman whose duty it is to take care of the rooms and make the beds in college. Female bedmakers were forbidden in Cambridge in 1625, but are now usual.
{{smaller block|The ''bed-makers'' are the women who take care of the rooms; there is about one to each staircase, that is to say, to every eight rooms.{{right|''C. A. Bristed'', English University, p. 30.}}}}

'''bedmate''' (bed′māt), ''n.'' A bedfellow.   ''Shak.''

'''bed-molding''' (bed′mōl″ding), ''n.'' In ''arch.'', a molding of the cornice of an entablature, situated beneath the corona and immediately above the frieze. Also called ''bedding-molding.''

'''bedote†''' (bē-dōt′), ''v. t.''   [ME., < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dote.'']   To make to dote; befool; deceive.
{{smaller block|For to ''bedote'' this queene was her entent.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1547.}}}}

'''Bedouin''' (bed′ö-in), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Early mod. E. ''Bedwin'', or as ML. ''Baduini, Beduini'', pl. (ME. rarely ''Bedoynes''); mod. E. also freq. ''Bedoween'', and more exactly ''Bedawi'', sing., ''Bedawin'', pl., after Ar., the form ''Bedouin'' being < F. ''Bédouin'' (OF. ''Beduin'' = It. ''Beduino'', ML. ''Beduinus'', etc.), < Ar. ''badawīn'', pl. of ''badawīy'', a dweller in the desert (cf. ''badāwi'', rural, rustic), < ''badw'', desert, open country.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' An Arab of the desert; one of the nomadic Arabs, divided into many tribes, who live in tents, rear flocks and herds, especially of camels, and are scattered over Arabia, parts of Syria, and Egypt and other parts of Africa. Also ''Bedawi'', plural ''Bedawin.''
{{smaller block|Professionally, and in the ordinary course of their lives, ''Bedouins'' are only shepherds and herdsmen: their raids on each other, or their exploits in despoiling travellers and caravans, are but occasional, though welcome and even exciting, exceptions to the common routine.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 246.}}}}

'''2.''' A vagabond boy; a street Arab.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Relating to the Bedouins.

'''bed-pan''' (bed′pan), ''n.'' '''1.''' A pan for warming beds; a warming-pan.—'''2.''' A necessary utensil for the use of persons confined to bed.

'''bedpheer†, bedphere†,''' ''n.'' Erroneous spellings of ''bedfere.''

'''bed-plate, bed-piece''' (bed′plāt, -pēs), ''n.'' In ''mech.'', the sole-plate or foundation-plate of an engine, etc.

'''bedpost''' (bed′pōst), ''n.'' '''1†.''' Same as ''bedstaff.''—'''2.''' A post forming an angle of a bedstead, in old bedsteads often rising high enough to support the canopy and rods for the curtain.—{{smaller|'''In the twinkling of a bedpost,''' with the utmost rapidity. See ''bedstaff.''}}

'''bed-presser''' (bed′pres″ėr), ''n.'' A lazy fellow; one who loves his bed.
{{smaller block|This sanguine coward, this ''bed-presser'', this horse-back breaker, this huge hill of flesh. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.}}}}

'''bedquilt''' (bed′kwilt), ''n.'' A wadded and quilted covering for a bed. Also used for ''bedspread'' and ''comforter.''
{{smaller block|The king [in a Sicilian fairy-story] issues a proclamation promising a large reward to whoever shall steal the ''bed-quilt'' of a certain ogre.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 34.}}}}

'''bedrabble''' (bē-drab′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drabble.'']   To make wet and dirty with rain and mud.   ''Kingsley.''

'''bedraggle''' (bẹ̄-drag′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''draggle.'']   To soil or wet by dragging in dirt, mud, moist places, etc., as the bottom of a garment in walking; cause to appear wet and limp, as a flag when rained upon.

'''bedral<sup>1</sup>''' (bed′ral), ''n.''   [Also ''bethral, betherel''; appar. a corruption of ''beadle'', var. ''beddel'', Sc. ''beddal'', etc.]   A beadle. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|I’ll hae her before presbytery and synod; I’m half a minister mysel’, now that I’m ''bedral'' in an inhabited parish.
{{right|''Scott'', Bride of Lammermoor, xxxiv.}}}}

'''bedral<sup>2</sup>†''' (bed′ral), ''n.''   [Also ''bedrel'', a corruption of ''bedred'', for ''bedrid'': see ''bedrid.'']   A person who is bedridden.   ''Knox.'' Also ''bed-thrall.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>His father—who as ''Bedrel'' lay
Before his gate. {{right|''Douglas'', tr. of Virgil.}}</poem>}}

'''bedreint†.''' Obsolete past participle of ''bedrench.''

'''bedrench''' (bẹ̄-drench′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bedrenchen'' (pp. ''bedreint''); < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drench.'']   To drench thoroughly; soak; saturate with moisture.
{{smaller block|Receyve our billes with teres al ''bedreynt.''
{{right|''Court of Love'', l. 577.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Such crimson tempest should ''bedrench''
The fresh green lap of fair King Richard’s land.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 3.}}}}

'''bedress''' (bẹ̄-dres′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''dress.'']   To dress up.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Bride whose tonish inclination
Attended to the ruling fashion,
To make her entry had ''bedress’d''
Her upright form in all her best.</poem>
{{right|''W. Combe'', Dr. Syntax in Search of a Wife, v.}}}}

'''bedridden, bedrid''' (bed′rid″n, -rid), ''a.''   [< ME. ''bedred, bedrede, bedreden, bedredden,'' adj. and n., < AS. ''bedreda, bedrida, bedryda, beddredda,'' n., one bedridden, lit. a bed-rider (< ''bed,'' bed, + ''rida, ridda,'' a rider, a knight, < ''rīdan,'' ride). Cf. LG. ''bedderede, bedderedig,'' bedridden; OHG. ''pettiriso,'' G. ''bettrise,'' of same sense. The second element came to be regarded as the pp. of ''ride;'' hence the now usual form ''bedridden,'' ME. ''bedreden.'']   Confined to bed by age, infirmity, or sickness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Is not your father grown incapable
Of reasonable affairs? . . .
Lies he not ''bed-rid?'' {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3.}}</poem>
What an over-worne and ''bedrid'' Argument is this!
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
{{smaller block|Old ''bedridden'' palsy. {{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}

'''bed-right†, bed-rite†''' (bed′rīt), ''n.''   [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''right, rite.'']   The privilege of the marriage-bed.
{{smaller block|<poem>No ''bed-right'' [in some eds. ''bed-rite''] shall be paid
Till Hymen’s torch be lighted.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}

'''bedrip†''', ''n.''   [ME., also ''bedripe, bedrepe'', etc., < AS. ''bedrīp'', < ''bedu'', prayer, + ''rīp'', a reaping: see ''bead'' and ''reap''. Also called in AS. ''bēnrīp'', < ''bēn'', prayer, + ''rīp''.]   Boon-work at harvest-time: a service which some tenants had to perform at the bidding or request of their lord.

'''bed-rite†''', ''n.'' See ''bed-right.''

'''bed-rock''' (bed′rok), ''n.''   [< ''bed''<sup>1</sup> + ''rock.'']   '''1.''' In ''mining'', the older crystalline and slaty rocks which underlie the unconsolidated gravelly and volcanic beds of Tertiary and Post-tertiary ages, along the flanks of the Sierra Nevada. {{smaller|The term is beginning to be used elsewhere to designate solid rock lying under loose detrital masses, such as sand and gravel.}} Hence—'''2.''' That which underlies anything else, as a foundation; bottom layer; lowest stratum.
{{smaller block|Everywhere life and energy, working on a gigantic scale, have plowed furrows into the institutional ''bed rock'' of Western Society.
{{right|''C. H. Shinn'', Land Laws of Mining Districts, p. 44.}}}}

'''bedroom''' (bed′röm), ''n.'' '''1.''' Room in a bed; sleeping-room in bed. [In this sense properly with a hyphen.]
{{smaller block|Then by your side no ''bed-room'' me deny.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 3.}}}} 2. A room or apartment containing or intended to contain a bed; a sleeping-apartment.

'''bedrop''' (bē-drop′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bedropped'' (sometimes ''bedropt''), ppr. ''bedropping''.   [< ME. ''bedroppen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''drop''.]   '''1.''' To drop upon; fall upon in drops.
{{smaller block|<poem>As men sene the dew ''bedroppe''
The leves and the flowers eke.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., iii. 254.}}}}
'''2.''' To cover, strew, or sprinkle with drops, or as if with drops; bespatter; bespangle.
{{smaller block|<poem>The yellow carp, in scales ''bedropp’d'' with gold.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 144.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Rueful cheek,
Pale and ''bedropped'' with ever-flowing tears.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, ix.}}}}

'''bed-sacking''' (bed′sak″ing), ''n.'' Canvas designed to be stretched on the framework of a bedstead to support the mattresses and bedclothes.

'''bed-screw''' (bed′skrö), ''n.'' '''1.''' A bed-key or bed-wrench.—'''2.''' Same as ''barrel-screw''.

'''bedside''' (bed′sīd), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bedsyde'', orig. ''beddes side'', i. e., bed’s side.]   The side of a bed; position by a bed: usually with reference to attendance on one confined to bed: as, she watched by his ''bedside'' till dawn.
